analysis.one_liner: Requires banks, brokers, insurers, and credit bureaus to safeguard customer data and stop sharing it without notice.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 1998, referred to committee and then a subcommittee, drew zero cosponsors, and died there when the Congress ended in January 1999 without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written financial privacy rules into law: banks, brokers, insurers, credit card issuers, and credit bureaus would be legally required to protect the security and confidentiality of customer records, collect only information they actually need, and stop handing customer data to third parties for their own use unless the transaction required it or the customer was told and given a chance to say no. Customers would gain the right to sue for at least $500 plus attorney's fees when a company knowingly leaked their information and caused real harm. The bill never reached a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a bank account, credit card, mortgage, brokerage account, insurance policy, or credit file — effectively nearly every American adult. They would gain legal protection against having their account data, Social Security number, and personal details sold or passed to third parties, a right to accurate records, mandatory security safeguards against hackers and identity thieves, and the ability to sue in federal court with attorney's fees when a company knowingly mishandles their data.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an affirmative legal duty on financial institutions to respect customer privacy and to build administrative, technical, and physical safeguards protecting records from threats, hazards, and unauthorized access.

Bars financial institutions from disclosing customer financial or personal information to third parties for their independent use, except to complete a customer-initiated transaction, at the customer's request, under legal process, or after clear notice giving the customer the right to deny the disclosure.

Limits collection to information actually needed to run the customer's relationship, requires prompt correction of inaccurate records, restricts employee access to data, and requires third parties receiving information to agree to keep it confidential.

Gives customers a private right to sue for at least $500 (or actual damages if greater) plus court costs and attorney's fees when a company knowingly violates the law and causes substantial injury, and prohibits companies from writing waiver clauses into their contracts to escape these obligations.

Covers virtually the whole financial sector — banks, brokers, insurers, loan companies, credit card issuers, and nationwide credit bureaus — with enforcement by the FTC and the sector's regulators, and preserves stronger state privacy laws.

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions bear the cost: building and maintaining security systems, retraining staff, redesigning data practices, and giving up revenue from selling or sharing customer information. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to customers through fees, and banks would argue that restricting data flows raises their costs of detecting fraud and marketing products.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on institutions of every size, from national banks to small community banks and credit unions, and some of that cost would predictably be passed on to customers through fees.

Restricting the flow of customer data cuts against practices financial firms use to detect fraud, verify identities, and market products, so the rules would create friction in ordinary transactions as well as protecting against abuse.

The $500 statutory minimum per violation, plus attorney's fees, creates broad litigation exposure for any company that knowingly misses a requirement — a real cost that an honest supporter would have to acknowledge even while defending the remedy as the teeth of the bill.
Enforcement is split across the FTC, the banking regulators, the SEC, the CFTC, and others, which invites inconsistent rules and gaps in coverage across the many types of institutions covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to customers are concrete and broad: a legal duty to protect records, an effective right to stop third-party data sharing, error correction, and a workable lawsuit remedy that ordinary people could actually afford to use because of fee-shifting. The costs — compliance spending and reduced data-sharing revenue — fall mainly on the industry, with some likely pass-through to consumers in fees and some friction in fraud detection and marketing. The bill was not cheap or frictionless, but its design (model disclosures, agency regulations, safe harbor for using them, preservation of stronger state laws) is a serious attempt at balance; the drawbacks are real but modest next to the privacy and identity-theft protections gained.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Banking Committee and then to its financial institutions subcommittee, and it sat there with no cosponsors and no action until the Congress ended in January 1999 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce of New York, the ranking Democrat on the House Banking and Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on August 4, 1998, near the end of the two-year Congress.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services, and the next day, August 5, 1998, to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions that profit from collecting, sharing, and selling customer data are better off, because no privacy mandate, security requirement, or customer lawsuit right ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that share customer data

for.role: Ranking Member, House Committee on Banking and Financial Services

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Banks, brokers, insurers, and credit bureaus
against.what_they_did: Opposed standalone privacy mandates that would restrict sharing and selling of customer data during this period

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House, so its support never got a chance to register.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from disclosing customer information to third parties for independent use without notice and a customer's chance to opt out, and would require costly security safeguards. Their interest in unrestricted data use runs against customers' privacy in this bill.

industries.industry: Nationwide credit reporting agencies and data brokers
industries.note: Explicitly covered as financial institutions, they would lose their ability to compile and disseminate consumer information without the new restrictions, accuracy duties, and lawsuit exposure. Their business model is built on the data flows the bill would restrict.
Covered under the bill's broad definition, they would face SEC enforcement of the same privacy and disclosure duties; firms that share or sell client information would bear the compliance cost.
Covered as financial institutions, they would be restricted in sharing policyholder personal information — including name changes, addresses, and family data — with third parties and affiliates.
